newsitem.title: USA: Oil cos still wait to hear fate of Burma projects.
newsitem.headline: Oil cos still wait to hear fate of Burma projects.

text.p: U.S. oil companies were still waiting to hear the fate of their Burma projects after President Bill Clinton on Tuesday signed into law unilateral sanctions against the Rangoon regime.
"At this point, we still believe the projects we've signed will be able to continue," said Unocal Corp spokesman Barry Lane, after the White House announcement.
The executive order signed by President Clinton on Tuesday was expected after Secretary of State Madeleine Albright announced the administration's intention to do so last month.
The order in general terms prohibits "United States persons from new investment in Burma" and becomes law from 0001 EDT on May 21.

However, at what point new investment in projects will be halted by the sanctions is open to the interpretation of the Treasury Departement's Office of Foreign Asset Control (OFAC), which is charged with implementing the sanctions.

There are around 20 U.S.-based companies with direct ivnestment or employees in Burma, according to Washington-based Investor Responsibility Research Center, a non-profit think tank funded mainly by institutional and public sector investors.

Most are involved in the oil and gas sector and the main question facing the three largest oil companies invested in Burma -- Unocal, Texaco Inc and Atlantic Richfield Co -- is at what point they must stop investing.

Unocal expects it will be allowed to continue with its Yadana project to bring natural gas from offshore Burma onshore, mainly to Thailand. The $1.2 billion scheme, in which Unocal has a 28.26 percent stake, is already well advanced in the construction stage.

But the company also has a contract to explore and develop the M8 block adjacent to the Yadana field offshore Burma, a project which would take major new investment, as well as other gas transport and distribution contracts.

Texaco is operator and holds a 42.9 percent share in the Yetagun gas field, located 125 miles off Burma's western coast in the Indian Ocean. It is currently being commercially evaluated and may involve major investment in a pipeline to carry gas to Thailand.
A Texaco official said that its lawyers in Washington were expecting to hear from OFAC offiicals Tuesday night about the fate of their projects.
Los Angeles-based ARCO has invested $30 million dollars in two offshore exploration blocks, though it has yet to determine if they are commercially viable.

"Our belief is that we can advance with our efforts...(but publication of OFAC's rules) would give us a better understanding of how the executive order is being interpreted," said ARCO spokesman Al Greenstein.
